questions.q: Define irony and symbolism in your own words, giving one example from daily life for each.
questions.a: Irony: a situation where the outcome is opposite to what is expected or intended (e.g., a fire station burning down). Symbolism: an object representing a deeper idea (e.g., a wilting tulsi plant symbolising a family's declining health). A wrong answer that swaps the definitions or gives only literary examples shows the student cannot distinguish the conceptual core from textual instances.

questions.q: In the chapter, the phrase "mtkM+w lH;rk" (industrial development) is repeated. Explain why this repetition functions as verbal irony.
questions.a: The phrase is verbally ironic because each repetition occurs alongside descriptions of poisoned water, dead trees, and displaced villagers — the exact opposite of "development". A student who merely says "it is repeated" misses the contrast between label and reality; a student who calls it situational irony confuses the device type.

questions.q: Compare the irony in the author's description of the "ekyo èkjrh xgu xaHkhj" (past beauty) with the irony in the villagers' acceptance of pollution. How do they differ in target and effect?
questions.a: The first is authorial verbal irony targeting the reader's nostalgia — the past beauty is invoked only to sharpen the present horror. The second is situational irony targeting the villagers' complicity — they endure pollution because they believe it brings livelihood. A conflated answer reveals inability to distinguish irony's subtypes and their rhetorical aims.

questions.q: Critique the view that the chapter's symbolism is "heavy-handed" because every natural element stands for loss. Defend or refute with two textual points.
questions.a: Refute: (1) Symbols evolve — the river first symbolises abundance, later betrayal, showing layered meaning. (2) The author juxtaposes symbols (e.g., "unh&ukys" warmth/coolness vs. "ckofM+;k¡" factory smoke) creating tension, not monotony. A student who agrees without textual support shows evaluative weakness; one who lists symbols without analysing their progression misses the nuance.

questions.q: Write a four-line Hindi stanza that uses one symbol from the chapter to express the irony of "development" in your own neighbourhood.
questions.a: Example: "धुएँ की चादर ओढ़े नदी / कारखाने की 'प्रगति' बनी / आम का ठूंठ पूछे चुपके / 'विकास' कहाँ, विनाश यहाँ?" A poor answer uses no symbol or states the irony directly ("development is bad") instead of embodying it through imagery.
